prompt.context: You are sitting in one of Chicago's oldest scotch bars with a fellow intern. It is a Friday night after a busy week at your summer internship. The weather is mild—a perfect summer evening. While enjoying one of the bar's finest stogies and sipping an 18-year old McCallen single malt, your friend asks you how much you think the bar is worth.
prompt.question: Using a back-of-the-envelope calculation, how would you go about determining the value of this bar?

clarifying_info.a: The bar sells two things: liquor and cigars. The average cost of a cigar is $9 and the average cost of a drink is $12.

clarifying_info.q: What is the capacity of the bar?

clarifying_info.a: The bar is located on one of Chicago's busier streets for foot traffic.
The bar is open Tuesday through Sunday from 5 pm until 2 am.

clarifying_info.q: How many staff does the bar have?
clarifying_info.a: A bartender, a waiter, and a waitress — all three were there the entire evening.

clarifying_info.q: What discount rate should I use?
clarifying_info.a: The discount rate typically used for bars of this genre is 13%.

clarifying_info.q: What is the annual growth rate of cash flows?
clarifying_info.a: The bar's cash flow is growing at 3% — the rate of inflation.

exhibits.title: Daily Sales
exhibits.shows: A table showing daily sales benchmarks for the bar across two day-type categories (Fridays & Saturdays vs. Rest of Week) and two seasonal periods (Spring & Summer vs. Fall & Winter).

framework: Estimate annual revenue: segment by day type (Fri/Sat vs. rest of week) and season (spring/summer vs. fall/winter)
Estimate annual costs: split into variable costs (% of revenue) and fixed costs
Calculate EBIT = Revenue - Variable Costs - Fixed Costs
Apply tax rate to get after-tax free cash flow
Apply growing perpetuity formula: Value = CF / (r - g) to arrive at business valuation

questions.prompt: What drives variation in daily revenues?
questions.guidance: Days of the week (Fridays and Saturdays are typically busier) and seasonality (people tend to be out more during summer than winter). The candidate should identify these two dimensions before or upon receiving Exhibit 1.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate total annual revenues.
questions.guidance: Candidate should build up revenues by multiplying daily sales figures by the number of days in each bucket, then sum all four buckets. Watch for realistic assumptions and logical progression. The correct total is $568,000.

math.setup: Year = 50 operating weeks (bar closed Mondays; open Tue–Sun = 6 days/week). Spring & Summer = 25 weeks; Fall & Winter = 25 weeks. Two day types: Fri & Sat (2 days/week), Rest of Week (4 days/week).
steps: Fri & Sat, Spring/Summer: $4,800 x 2 days = $9,600/week; $9,600 x 25 weeks = $240,000
Rest of Week, Spring/Summer: $4,800 x (1/6) x 4 days = $3,200/week; $3,200 x 25 weeks = $80,000

questions.prompt: Estimate annual costs (fixed and variable) and calculate pre-tax income.
questions.guidance: Variable costs: 20% of revenues. Fixed costs: $120,000 (rent, maintenance, management, insurance, liquor license, employees). Pre-tax income = Revenue - Variable Costs - Fixed Costs.

math.setup: Revenue = $568,000; Variable costs = 20% x $568,000; Fixed costs = $120,000

questions.guidance: Apply the 40% tax rate to pre-tax income to arrive at the after-tax cash flow figure used in the DCF.

steps: Round to $200,000 for ease of calculation

questions.prompt: How do you value the bar? Perform the valuation.
questions.guidance: A great candidate will proactively recognize that the value is the present value of all future cash flows. Use the growing perpetuity formula CF / (r - g). Discount rate = 13%, growth rate = 3%, so r - g = 10%.

math.answer: The bar is worth approximately $2 million

brainstorming.prompt: What are possible fixed costs and variable costs for this bar?

categories.name: Variable Costs
ideas: Cost of goods sold (liquor and cigars — 20% of revenue)

recommendation: Using a discounted cash flow (growing perpetuity) approach, the Scotch Bar is worth approximately $2 million
This is based on estimated annual after-tax cash flows of ~$200,000, a discount rate of 13%, and a 3% perpetual growth rate
risks: Revenue estimates rely on assumptions about occupancy and spending that may not hold
Seasonality and weekday traffic patterns could shift with economic conditions or neighborhood changes
Key-man risk: the bar's reputation may depend on specific staff or ownership
Regulatory risk: liquor license renewal or changes in smoking ordinances
next_steps: Verify actual revenue figures and occupancy data from the bar's financial records
Benchmark against comparable bar/restaurant transactions in the Chicago market
Assess lease terms and renewal risk as a key driver of long-term cash flow stability
